utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are no preliminaries, so, therefore, could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I will deal with a few matters. The first. The Prosecution has informed the Chamber and the Defence through an informal communication, which is hereby on the record, that it would not seek leave to re-call witnesses Corbic or Lekovic. Witness Corbic had been given an instruction not to speak to anyone about his testimony pending the Prosecution's final position on a possible re-call, and, accordingly, VWS is hereby instructed to inform Witness Corbic that the given instruction is now lifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday. That is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And Mr. Bakrac will now continue his examination. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagic, good morning. Mr. Gagic, yesterday before we finished for the day, you said how, in 1991, you were an inspector and that later you were given a rank, that this was in late 1993 or early 1994, when ranks were introduced to the State Security Department. Are you able to tell us which rank you received?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first rank that I received was major. Later, I was lieutenant-colonel, then colonel, and I retired with the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us when the State Security Department introduced ranks?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that ranks were introduced to the State Security Department quite late, in comparison to the public security department. I think that this happened some four or five, or even more, years later than in the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say four, five years later, are you able to more closely state the time-period?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was sometime in 1996 or 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, I would now like to focus on early 1991 and the crisis in Yugoslavia at the time. Was there any situation in 1991 at the public security department of the MUP that was specific at that time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in 1991, or, actually, even in late 1990, policemen from Croatia began to arrive at the MUP who had lost their jobs, either because they left the service on their own, or because they were dismissed from their jobs because of some violations which the Croatian authorities at the time believed to be serious violations of work duty but, in fact, were just minor infringements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And were you interested to know what was going on; and was there any kind of recommendation in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did become interested for a number of reasons. First of all, it was the nature of my work, even before, to communicate with large number of policemen from other republics as well, from Macedonia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro. Property crimes are crimes of such a nature that criminals commit crimes throughout the whole territory and police co-operation was absolutely necessary, even privately. There was private conversation, telephone calls, exchange of information, other than the official forms of communication or co-operation. So that I knew a large number of policemen who were in Croatia and a number of those policemen came to Serbia. I became personally interested because the majority of them contacted me, asking me to help them to resolve their status. I was personally interested and then the position was taken by the MUP of Serbia leadership to allow those policemen to receive employment relatively quickly without going through the entire procedures to be admitted by fulfilling all the requirements and going through the regular procedure, but without having to wait very long for this to be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say the decision was taken at the highest level, what are you thinking of? Who made this decision on the employment of these policemen?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was made by the minister of the interior but it was in the form of a recommendation. It wasn't -- or at least I don't know that decision was made in the form of a binding order or anything like that. It was done in the form of a recommendation for people who were already policemen and who were without work to be admitted and for them to just continue with work, to receive assistance with accommodation. Actually, to help them normalise relations. This was done by the minister because the policemen did not only come to Belgrade. These policemen from Croatia were arriving in Novi Sad, Kragujevac. So this was a decision at the level of the ministry, or the recommendation, and it did not apply only to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, I would now ask you to look at a document; D303. And while we're waiting --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I was just about to say that. It is under seal, so I would like to move into private session for this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know -- actually over the break I will check why it is MFI'd and we will see if we are going to be tendered or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is still a provenance issue pending. And that is, I think D303 was obtained from Mr. Stanisic and that the Stanisic Defence was trying to obtain a copy from the -- an official copy from the Serb authorities. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, let me repeat the question since we've discussed other issues in the meantime. Can you date this footage, when it was that Mr. Kostic, vice-president of the SFRY Presidency, came to Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging from the footage, I'd say that it took place a month or two later; sometime in the month of July of 1991. I say that because of the historic date referred to by Branko Kostic. I also base my assessment on the fact that he said that he had just come over from that other gathering. So I guess it must be the month of July. At any rate, a couple of months after the events in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does this video-clip indicate that at least some members of the SFRY Presidency had given their support?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the discussions we heard do indicate that the President of the Presidency is promising to the people there that he would provide them with protection. So this was no political campaigning, where promises are given. Rather, people are given promises that they would be protected from an escalation of conflicts and that they would be provided safety to alleviate the fears that they felt towards the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can 2D1055.1 become admitted. But maybe MFI'd until my Case Manager produces the Registry with a disc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any possibility to MFI a document, Madam Registrar, if you don't have the underlying material? That is possible, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then the number to be assigned Madam Registrar would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document -- video 2D1055.1 will receive number D690.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we now look at another video-clip, which I believe follows precisely up on what you said. This is 2D1055.2 from the same batch of materials disclosed to us by the Prosecution. And the time is 4 minutes, 7 seconds to 6 minutes, 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Branko Kostic: Europe and the world remember those policies very well. I'm convinced that Europe and the world will finally realise today what this policy means and the disastrous effects that such a policy could have, not only for the Serbian people in this territory of Croatia which is most directly threatened but also the consequences that such a policy could have in Europe in general. "Our federal organs, particularly the Federal Executive Council, have so far seriously concealed this topic as the circumstances are as they are. It is about the endangered area and where the Serbian people are suffering, but the Federal Executive Council does not care less. In this and in all of the other cases, it is must be reported to full extent and material-wise regardless of the ethnic composition of population to which the disaster happened. "We will do everything in our power in order for the JNA, which is strong, powerful, which has the wherewithal, now more than ever, that it may offer help and support to all the parts of the people who will be endangered or already are, regardless of where they are situated. "Today it is the Serbian people in Croatia who are at risk, and should the events develop in such a way as no one would wish to, we do not exclude the possibility that some other people may be endangered in some other areas and our army must be the force as a proper national army that will protect each and every one of our endangered citizens, regardless of their nationality, religious affiliation or political orientation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, before you ask questions, the Chamber wonders to what extent it would assist to see all the details of what Mr. Kostic is telling here. First of all, is there any dispute about Kostic going to that area approximately that time and in support of the Serb cause at that moment and giving -- delivering speeches, giving political support.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We do not dispute what is seen in the video, which I think supports Your Honour's assertion, but we just do not dispute that he made this speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check what you ... It's not entirely clear to me, Ms. Friedman. You say you do not dispute what is seen in the video but you just do not assert he made what speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We -- we resist agreeing to facts which we cannot check in great detail on the spot, but we do not dispute the authenticity of this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, the exact words, reading that and asking the witness whether this indicates that someone from the Presidency came to give support, I mean, that's clear. If he is vice-president, of course, he is coming -- what exactly are we supposed to learn from this? What are you exactly establishing? The specific words, or that he was there, or that there was political support or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to buttress our case, and to challenge the case of the Prosecution that, in 1991, joint criminal enterprise commence, one in which my client participated, I want to depict a situation where the Presidency of the SFRY was still operational. And not only that. It got engaged - and the witness will speak about it - through the presence of the JNA as a dominant force in Slavonia, and this is the better part of the indictment against my client. In the relevant part, it is stated that he substantially supports, assists, and participates in the joint criminal enterprise which was reflected in the crimes committed in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will not stop you. But to say that it's convinced that it greatly assists to look at this material to reach conclusions, as you suggested, is -- that would be an overstatement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not going to exaggerate. I have finished there. I simply wanted to show and illustrate the genesis of how this witness was engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gagic, after these addresses by Mr. Kostic, were there any movements, shifts, and did the Yugoslav People's Army come out of its barracks?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already, it was noted in that period that the Yugoslav People's Army was taking a more active role in the protection of the civilian population and was actually becoming the only factor of protection of the civilian population along with the self-organisation of the local population. This is a period when the forming of the TO staffs began in that territory, when the -- when some other systems began to function within the military functions for the purpose of protecting the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You were -- we are talking these clips that we saw. You said it was July 1991. After July 1991, did the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, in a way, get involved in the activities; and, if it did, in what way? Activities relating to the protection of the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian MUP was not authorised to participate actively and directly in terms of its presence in the territory of the Republic of Croatia for the protection of the Serbian population, so that everything that was possibly done in terms of protection and had to do with the MUP of Serbia was done through the authorised military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the forming of some units occur which were sent to that area as part of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some two months later, approximately, two units were formed. I note -- or I emphasise these were volunteer units at the level of the Belgrade SUP. Actually, at the level of the Ministry of the Interior, but this was done from employees working at the Belgrade SUP, primarily from staff who voluntarily joined those units. And they -- before they worked in the Belgrade SUP, they had worked in the area of the Republic of Croatia. These were policemen who were dismissed or who had left their jobs, had been given jobs in the Belgrade SUP. Now they joined these volunteer units. One of those two units went to Knin and the other one, the other unit went to Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that these two units, which they joined as volunteers, mostly comprised policemen who, before that, were thrown out of Croatia, and then, after that, had gotten jobs in Belgrade. And, if so, were there any people who did not hail from Croatia, were not thrown out of Croatia, but did join these police units? Were there such people?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit that I myself joined had just two of us who were not originally from Croatia and were not previously policemen in Croatia. I had spent my whole work history in Serbia. There was another man who came from Krusevac and who worked in one of the police stations in the Belgrade area. All the other members - and there were some 40 of us - were members of the Croatian police force who had become unemployed of their own free will due to threats or were dismissed. They had come to Belgrade, and then, after that, had joined this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Based on what you know, are you able to tell us, other than these two units, you say one went to Knin and then this one of yours to Slavonia, were there any other units or any other members of the Serbian MUP who went to Slavonia in an organised manner or not?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for them going to Slavonia in an organised way, at that time, there were no other such units or any other formations. I am not ruling out the possibility that, individually, for a day or two or for a weekend or for the odd holiday day, policemen went from Serbia, if they hailed from such an area, they went to visit their families and things like that. As for them leaving in an organised way, for the purposes of protecting the population over there, no one else went from Serbia other than those two units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And these two units, are you able to tell us which sector they belonged to in the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both units belonged to the public security department, and they comprised policemen who were employed at the Belgrade SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We're going to focus on this unit that went to Slavonia, and from what I understand, you went with the unit. First, my question is this: You went to that area as what sort of formation?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't want it to seem if I overlooked that deliberately. When we're talking about the departure of these units, I thought that this would imply but perhaps it is important for me to say that. In the area of Slavonia, a number of SAJ, "Specijalna Antiteroristicka Jedinica," special anti-terrorist units, headed by Radovan Stojicic, Badza, were already there in Slavonia. So when I said that I did not know whether any other units had been sent, I had said no, but this part of the special anti-terrorist unit was sent there before. So it was already present there. So I just want to avoid any misunderstanding about that or I don't want it to seem as if I did not mention that deliberately. Now I'm going to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First of all, you said SAJ, special anti-terrorist unit, which department did that belong to?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SAJ unit, special anti-terrorist unit, belonged to the public security. It always belonged to public security, and it still today belongs to public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And this unit, you say that it left before you. You mentioned Radovan Stojicic, Badza. Did the whole unit leave or did they go in another way; and, if they did, how many of them went?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a part of the unit went. It wasn't the whole unit. I think it was maybe some 15 or 20 members. Policemen that belonged to that unit. They would rotate. At some point, there were more of them, at some point fewer. But it was between 10 and 15 specials, or rather, policemen of that unit. They were permanently present. Partially they participated in the execution of combat actions, and they also worked on the security of the TO headquarters and personal security of Radovan Stojicic, Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We moved away from the topic a little bit, my question before that. I'm not criticising you. You wanted to explain this in order to avoid misunderstandings. My question was: This unit of volunteers from the MUP that we talked about, these members, former policemen from Croatia, and in what? What sort of formation was this? Was this a police formation?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately upon joining that unit, we were informed that we're going to be a military police company. Thus, that we're not going to be going there by establishment as members of the Ministry of the Interior, but that we're going to be a company of the military police of the Novi Sad Corps. This implied that we should not take our official IDs with us, that we should take our military booklets with us instead that we had in our possession. And immediately upon arriving in the area of Slavonia, we received official military IDs issued by the Novi Sad Corps, which was signed by General Bratic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, when you left Belgrade, did you leave as a group; and, if you did, were you issued any equipment in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left Belgrade in an organised manner as a group with an already established command structure of a company. We took with us our personal side-arms, which we already had as MUP employees. I specifically had just a pistol. And we were issued with uniforms which were blue, and they were a little bit atypical compared to the already prevalent green military uniforms and green camouflage military uniforms. However, these blue uniforms were there because, first of all, we were the police; and, secondly, these were made from thick serge material and since winter was coming, they were the best suited for us to use during that first initial presence of ours at the front. We also had white cross-belts. This is a belt and cross-belt that went over the shoulder as a symbol of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say blue uniforms, do you mean police blue uniforms, or what sort of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not the police blue uniforms. These were, in fact, winter uniforms of the fire brigade in Belgrade, which were perhaps taken out of service a year before that previously, and there were some left in supply. First of all, we wanted to use those uniforms; and, secondly, they were of best quality and because winter was coming up, they qualified as the most suitable to be issued to us. And the colour also suited the type of unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, we're talking about the winter that was approaching. When did this unit actually go to Eastern Slavonia and where did it go?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th, the unit was formed, and then on the 29th, it left. Our first destination was Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: For the transcript, we have to be more precise. You say the 28th it was formed and it left on the 29th. Which month was this and which year?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. The unit was formed on the 28th of September, 1991, and it left for Dalj, in Slavonia, on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First, are you able to tell us whether it was a departure of a secret nature; and, if not, who issued the permission? What sort of an agreement was reached about the sending of these volunteers from the MUP to Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forming of the unit and its departure to Slavonia was no secret, nor was there any reason for the formation of such a unit to be a secret. The permission for the unit to leave was given by the then-chief of the Secretariat of the Interior in Belgrade, Rade Markovic, and the then-minister of the interior at the time, Radmilo Bogdanovic. No, excuse me. No, it was already Zoran Sokolovic who was the minister of the interior already by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And as a company of the military police, when you crossed into Eastern Slavonia, as you said, did you have more duties, more assignments, still in the city SUP in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were touring the area engulfed by war, our work duties at the SUP were suspended, which meant that we could not have been engaged to work on the execution of any assignment for the needs of the city of Belgrade. We could not be summoned to return from the war-engulfed area in order to take part in any raids, arrests, or any similar activities. Simply, our duties were focussed within that military formation that we belonged to, and all of our duties were executed pursuant to the command and control system of the unit, whereas our work status remained unchanged in relation to the period. It was the same as we worked before. We had all the benefits as workers of the MUP. We had all the same benefits, as far as our years of service were calculated, salaries and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, and how did it come about that you decided to join the unit as a volunteer and go to Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My joining the unit and going to Slavonia was a personal act, on my part. There was no order that I received from anyone to do such a thing, nor was it a principle to go to such assignments, pursuant to an order. It was a personal act, action, and, in a way, I had already become a sympathiser and supporter of those people there, who, in my evaluation, were under serious threat in the Slavonia area and in the territory of Croatia as a whole. The choice to go to Slavonia was quite a coincidental thing. I wanted to help. I already had experience in police work, life experience, and I felt that I could make a much bigger contribution there than some young men of 20 or so who were going there as somebody who had to serve in the military, unprepared. It's a question as to how much training they had. This was a fact. I simply considered it to be a personal act of mine that I had to join and help those people, and simply by family tradition to participation in wars whenever Serbia was threatened was something that my ancestors also had done before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were policemen dispatched to any other crisis areas within Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an active crisis hotbed in Serbia, which was Kosovo. Before the outbreak of the conflict in Croatia, there were escalations of the conflict in Kosovo on a regular basis, so that a large part of the Serbian police force had to be dispatched to Kosovo for longer periods of time, such as a couple of months at the time. Thus, Serbia was in great difficulties at the time, in terms of not having sufficient policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You were in the public security department. Do you perhaps have any knowledge of any members of the State Security Department being dispatched to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: State security did have its structure in Kosovo, its branches and offices that were operational. Whenever there was a surge in conflicts, whenever public law and order was disrupted, they would reinforce their presence with contingents of policemen from other areas in Serbia. Otherwise, the police force that was present in Kosovo sufficed to deal with the situation without the policemen from other areas in Serbia coming to their aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, let us focus now on your story. You said that it was on the 29th of September, 1991, that you arrived in Vukovar. Where were you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 29 -- yes, the 29th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So where were you billeted when you arrived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we arrived in the village of Dalj on the 29th of September, we were put up in a daycare centre, a kindergarten to be precise. At that point in time, it was the only facility that could accommodate a 40-strong unit. We had to sleep on the floor, since the furnishings, of course, were appropriate for pre-school children. We had sleeping bags. We organised duty shifts in the perimeter of the facility we were billeted at. We also organised patrols --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, let's try to avoid what seems to confuse us. Page 23, line 16, your question was translated initially as: "You said that it was on the 29th of September, 1991, that you arrived in Vukovar." Then the interpreter corrected this and said: "29 -- yes, 29th of November, 1991."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was interpreter's mistake. So it is the 29th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we then continued with the 29th of September, I didn't know what -- so the correction was a mis-correction. Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, tell us, first of all, who was in command of your unit; and under whose command did you place yourselves upon your arrival in this village of Dalj?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit was under the command of the former commander of a special unit in Zagreb who had to leave the Croatian police under pressure. His name was Veljko Bogunovic. He was admitted to the Belgrade SUP where he worked for almost a year and -- so he was among the first who had to leave Croatia. He was the unit's commander. He had his deputies and his -- put the command and control structure of his unit in place. We placed ourselves under the control of the SAO -- SAO -- Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem TO staff, which was under the command of Radovan Stojicic, Badza. In fact, we placed ourselves under the command of the TO staff, but our immediate superiors were, in fact, the Novi Sad Corps. We were part of the Novi Sad Corps but locally were under the command of the TO staff commander, Radovan Stojicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, as you arrived in Dalj, were you issued with any weapons?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we took along our side-arms, but we were issued with certain weapons in Dalj as well. They were semi-automatic and automatic rifles. There was one, a machine-gun. These were rounds belonging to the military police company. Those were not weapons that had belonged to the civilian police. So that while we had taken along some of the weapons, we were issued with other weapons in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The weapons you were additionally given, Mr. Gagic, where did that happen and who handed the weapons over to you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received additional weapons in Dalj in the TO defence arms depot. Now, was this, at the same time, an arms depot for the entire Slavonia or only for the place of Dalj? Well, I think it was a central depot of the TO staff of the SAO Krajina and Baranja, though it was stationed in Dalj. That's what it was called. But it belonged to the central structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've noted the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start, but there was an urgent matter which required the attention of all three of us. Mr. Bakrac, are you ready to proceed? Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, Your Honour. Thank you. Let me first apologise. I omitted to tender 2D1055.2 into evidence, as an MFI'd exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to have 2D1055.2 to be marked for identification. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D691, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it will keep that status until we receive further information. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, before the break, we talked about the TO arms depot in Dalj. Do you have any knowledge about the possible sources of supplies for that TO arms depot in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I have, that particular depot received its supplies from other military depots of the JNA. And I can claim that because I saw, based on the sort of weapons that were there, such as Zoljas, hand-held rocket-launchers and the like, that they could only have been weapons belonging to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, how long did you stay in Dalj, in that daycare centre; and what were the tasks that you were performing?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent some 15 to 20 days in Dalj. It was roughly on the 20th of October, between the 15th and 20 October 1991, that we were relocated to Erdut. I've already said that the conditions in that daycare centre were not appropriate for a unit. During our stay in Dalj, we engaged in patrols and securing the facility where we were billeted. We had both car and pedestrian patrols which went as far as the villages around Dalj. We were, in fact, waiting for our next deployment, which was to be a continued and definitive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: While you were patrolling, did you carry any sort of identification papers with you; and, if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military records that we had, we left in the headquarters. We had on us military passes, passes of the military police that we had been given by the Novi Sad Corps command. This was to serve as our identification during the task that we performed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that we didn't catch the name of the general from the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The name of the general of the Novi Sad Corps, could you repeat the name of the general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was General Bratic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Gagic, this would be the convenient time. You say that the commander of the Novi Sad Corps, General Bratic, issued you with these papers. Did there come a time that a new commander was appointed at the head of the Novi Sad Corps; and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't call it a replacement. It was roughly in that period that General Bratic was killed. It was in early October of 1991. He was replaced by Andrija Biorcevic, a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, after having spent between 15 and 20 days in Dalj, were you deployed to a different location with a specific task given to the unit?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once we were given billeting quarters in Erdut, which were, in fact, a part of the Saponia company complex, we, as the unit, were given a specific task, which was to check the traffic across the Brotherhood and Unity bridge. That was the only road between Vojvodina and Eastern Slavonia, and we were supposed to check all the passengers, individuals travelling along that road, as well as the goods transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Until you were put up in the Saponia premises in Erdut, had any sort of facility been secured for you where you took your meals?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this particular facility belonging to Saponia did have a canteen, we had the premises but we didn't have the staff to man it. So before this was done, we took our meals in the 101st Recruitment Centre, which was, in fact, the so-called Arkan Centre, the Territorial Defence Centre. It was in that facility where Arkan's unit was billeted that we took our meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In these dozen or so days while you were taking your meals in the recruitment centre, did you have occasion to see Arkan and whomever it was who was stationed there?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we went on to have our meals there, I got to the know Arkan and Radovan Stojicic, Badza, though I had known Arkan from before on several different bases. I would also occasionally see Goran Hadzic coming to the centre, including, of course, members of Arkan's Volunteer Guard, who would take their meals there at the same time we did. And, of course, Radovan Stojicic who would come there periodically. It was not a centre that was closed off to the public, and other people were able to come there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to find out to which structure the Serbian Volunteer Guard and Arkan belonged, when they were there?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew from the very beginning that the Serbian Volunteer Guard and the volunteers who joined that guard were subordinated to the TO Staff, in terms of organisation, meaning to Radovan Stojicic, Badza, but they carried out tasks directly pursuant to orders of the Novi Sad Corps Command. So their tasks did not always imply that the order to execute the task or action planning proceeded through the TO Staff. There were also direct engagements by Novi Sad Corps units and through the TO Staff, but definitely they were resubordinated to the TO Staff and the TO Staff was resubordinated to the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, you say that, for a while, some ten days or so, you had your meals at this training centre and that you had been given a task to control the Bogojevski bridge as a unit. Are you able to tell us, if you know, how did the Serbian Volunteer Guard volunteers come to that particular area?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not spend too much time at the bridge. I was more involved in organisational tasks, but I did tour the deployed unit members at the bridge, and I had the opportunity to see when all sorts of formations arrived there, including the Serbian Volunteer Guard. They would arrive in a van. It was not a regular passenger vehicle. It was a van, a larger vehicle, with Belgrade plates. They would come in civilian clothing. New volunteers would come in civilian clothing, in civilian clothes, in small groups, three, four, five of them, meaning small groups, and the driver of the van was an older guard member, somebody who was already in the unit, thus, and he had a pass to cross that Erdut bridge. Thus, he had the permission to enter with the people who were with him in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know which structure was this permit to enter received from?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The permit was received from the TO Slavonia Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say that a few people would arrive in this van, you said, in civilian clothing. Did they have arms with them?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have weapons. They didn't even have side-arms that they perhaps had as citizens. They had to come without any weapons to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know where and when they were issued with weapons, once they arrived?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Volunteer Guard received its supplies from the TO Staff depot in Dalj. Because, once, we had the situation when I went for some additional equipment that we needed, and I saw a vehicle that belonged to the Guard that was also -- also being issued with some -- some weapons and ammunition, and then I could see that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was also being supplied through that depot, which received its supplies, in turn, from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity to hear or to see at the very beginning who trained? Or, rather, did the Serbian Volunteer Guard in Erdut carry out any kind of training?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Volunteer Guard did carry out training, even before we arrived, and after we arrived, the training was carried out as part of the activities of that centre. Behind the centre, there was a football field which was suitable for training. There was also an area which was suitable for target practice, infantry weapons target practice. I also know from talking with members of the SAJ unit that, in the beginning, these members of this unit were the instructors in Serbian Volunteer Guard, that it was they who trained the Serbian Volunteer Guard volunteers, Arkan's volunteers. They trained them during a period of time by training larger formations of 50 to 60 people and by providing special training for the most talented members of that Guard who later they appointed as instructors. So when the first cycle of training was over and when the first group of instructors was formed in the Serbian Volunteer Guard, they took over the training and the members of the SAJ no longer participated in this training, or conducted the training, and then other people would come to the Guard who already had special skills, whether they learned them in the army or because they were expert in martial arts. In any case --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the last sentence. What we have on our screen now is that: "And then other people would come to the Guard who already had special skills, whether they learned them in the army or because they were expert in martial arts ..." And then you added: "In any case ..." And what did then follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that was the end. That they were experts in martial arts who later continued to give the training. That was the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, this first thing, you said members of the SAJ unit. Let me repeat: Was the complete SAJ unit there out in the field?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A smaller part of it was out in the field. Less than a third of the total SAJ was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Without repeating it, earlier you explained how and with whom they came there as volunteers. Can you tell me just one more time, they belonged to which administration? Which department in the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SAJ were part of the public security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, we talked about arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at a document, which is already in evidence in this case. This is D31. I think that this is not under seal and that we can look at it in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Mr. Gagic, this is a document dated the 18th of October, 1991. 1st Military District. It's an information by the security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we haven't had a foundation as to the arming of Arkan's Men. I may have missed that. I would like to raise that though. In case that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to Mr. Bakrac. If there's no foundation, then, of course, the probative value is -- may be affected by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the document may be leading in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could we first address the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we first address the foundation and then look at the document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, we heard that this witness has personal knowledge about the arming and additional arming, and the arming of Arkan. The witness worked in the MUP. And before I show this document, I'm going to ask the witness if --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever, in the field, while you were staying, between October 1991 and April -- and April 1992, have knowledge as to whether Arkan and his Serbian Volunteer Guard were receiving weapons from the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have -- or didn't have such information. And in view of the type of weaponry, it's not very ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, did it have mines and explosive devices?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the MUP of the Republic of Serbia have Zoljas, Osas and military weapons at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now look at this information by the security organ of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Ms. Friedman, to say that there was nothing said about the base of knowledge. Of course, the witness testified that what he observed what happened at the depot where the Serbian Volunteer Guards received their supplies, where he said once they had a situation when he went for some additional, that he saw -- so there was some foundation, at least, for part of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believed it was a different unit, not the Serbian Volunteer Guard, but I would have go back to the spot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check that. Okay. If that's the case, then I may have been confused. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, what is being referred to here is information obtained through some lieutenant in the reserves. And can we focus on the second paragraph now where it says: "During several consecutive contacts with Arkan, the above named stated that the weaponry, ammunition and the MES mines and explosives had been supplied by the MUP and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia ..." I'm just going to stop here for a second just to ask you what the abbreviation, MES, M-E-S, stands for.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MES is an abbreviation for mines and explosives. These would be trip mines and other types of explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you again, did the MUP have these kind of explosive devices in its arsenal?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, it goes on to say here that this person found out from Arkan that he was distributing these devices to the TO Staffs of Erdut, Sarvas and Borovo Selo. And they say that records of the issued weapons should be kept and updated. Did you ever, during your stay in that area, have the opportunity to see or to hear that Arkan was distributing these weapons to the Erdut, Sarvas and Borovo Selo TOs?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that Arkan was in a position or that he had weapons and other combat equipment that he was distributing to the Territorial Defence. After all, he himself was directly being supplied through the Territorial Defence. So that in reading and looking at this document, I think that this is a re-telling of second-hand information, and the data seems to be inaccurate. It says here: In the former Erdut military training centre. That was never that centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gagic, did you have an opportunity while you were there to see what the relations between Arkan and the Novi Sad Corps were like?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan's relations with the Novi Sad Corps Command and lower-ranking officers of that corps was professional. It was quite decent. He conducted himself as a subordinate. He never strayed outside of the system and organisation for conducting armed conflict and armed combat, rather, he performed tasks as ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: While you were in Erdut, did you have the opportunity to see if anyone from the Novi Sad Corps came to that TO training centre in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I would see a number of officers from the Novi Sad Corps there. A couple of times, I also saw the security officer of the Novi Sad Corps, Colonel Kosutic. So he was the chief of the security organ of the Novi Sad Corps. I would see Generals Biorcevic and Ivanovic, and, later -- actually, I never had the opportunity to see General Bratic in person myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know where the command of the Novi Sad Corps was?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Novi Sad Corps was on a ship which was called Kozara. At the time, when I went to visit the ship on two occasions, it was in Erdut. It was anchored there. Whether it moved from that place, as it's a vessel, this is something that I could not assert.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance, as you told us that you were discharging military police duties, did you have an opportunity to see Arkan or his officers going to the Novi Sad Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I had the opportunity to see Arkan and his officers going to the Novi Sad Corps Command on several occasions, because I knew where the command was located, so I could see vehicles departing and people as well. These were lower-ranked officers and Arkan himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, during the time you spent in Erdut and -- both at the centre and later on when you moved to Saponia, did you see any officials of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia on the ground; or were you aware that he would come to visit Arkan and this Novi Sad Corps centre?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for Radovan Stojicic, Badza, who was on the ground anyway, I did not have an opportunity to see any of the higher-ranking representatives of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, do you know whether Radovan Stojicic, Badza, Arkan, and anyone else ever received any sort of award from the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that immediately after the termination of combat operations in Vukovar, perhaps five or six days later, after the termination of combat operations in Vukovar, the Novi Sad Corps Command distributed gifts to the deserving participants in the final operations in Vukovar. I believe that on that occasion there was a dinner held at the wine cellar of Saponia. That was the restaurant of the Saponia. Wine factory. I was present but I was not present during the distribution of these gifts because I was a bit late for the dinner because I had other obligations, and I'm not sure if that was the moment when these awards or gifts were given to them. These were weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I would like us to see 1D2309 while we are discussing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this should be under seal because -- or perhaps not. 1D2309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, if you say that it should perhaps be under seal or perhaps not, then, out of an abundance of caution, we'll put it under seal. But it would be appreciated if you would have prepared your position a bit more precisely. Please proceed. And this document provisionally is dealt with as a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. It seemed to me -- but I will check by the next break. I apologise for creating confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we move in private session for this purpose or not? I do not know what the possible reasons for confidentiality of the document are. Is this about content or about handwriting or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow -- I apologise. My only dilemma is that I believe that the provenance of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It comes from Mr. Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Try to find out. We provisionally will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We're aware of no reason it should be under seal and have the same information that the -- that it is from Mr. Stanisic. So unless the Defence team sees a reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you'll perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I have no further answers at this moment, but I can speak to Mr. Stanisic in the break and find out if there's anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not heard of any compelling reason why we should deal with it confidentially. Mr. Bakrac apparently doesn't know. Mr. Jordash has no specific reasons. Ms. Friedman can't tell us. We will deal with the document in open session unless you indicate that we should not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We can see no reason either for it to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we -- Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Just on a separate matter. There doesn't seem to be a translation uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then only part of the public will know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And we are aware that there was a translation in e-court previously provided by the Defence. But just on that note, we actually had it re-translated because there was a word that seemed inaccurate. So we could provide that by e-mail for the parties to upload perhaps in the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I do not know what the questions will be, but, of course, there should be a translation. Let's first listen to the questions that Mr. Bakrac will put.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if it may be of assistance, on page 2 of this document we can find the translation. This is how it was included in e-court, and this is information I got from my learned friend from the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gagic, the date is the 23rd -- the 12th Corps Command. The date is the 23rd of November, 1991, and the place is Dalj. And as we have the translation now, I will read it as it's a short document. "In sign of recognition for the successful co-operation and direct participation in combats for the liberation of Borovo, I am awarding the ... weapon as a war trophy to the most successful leaders of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem as follows. "Radovan Stojicic, Badza, the commander of the TO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, a hunting rifle, serial number ..." Number two, Zivko Trajkovic, deputy commander of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, a hunting rifle with the following serial number. "And, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, the commander of the special volunteers' squad of the TO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, a light machine-gun" with the following serial number. "Signed by the commander, Major-General, Andrija Biorcevic." Is this -- or was this the occasion and were these the awards that you mentioned which were distributed at a dinner held after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the weapons that were distributed and these were awards that were given out during the dinner. But as I said, I was not present during the distribution of the awards because I was late. But once I joined the dinner, I heard from those present that the commander of -- Major-General Andrija Biorcevic did distribute these weapons as gifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see my learned friend Mr. Jordash is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Only because I think this is already an exhibit, P3010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Then we shall move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, please tell us, after you transferred to Erdut, you told us that, in terms of organisation, you were in charge of the control of the Bogojevo bridge. Were you personally in charge of any other tasks or duties?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in addition to my occasional presence at the bridge and the assistance I provided to unit members when they needed it, I also had a role as an advisor and instructor. I was helping to constitute local police forces. When I say "the local police," what I mean is the Secretariat of the Interior Vukovar, with a seat in Dalj, and also the contacts that they needed to establish with already established police stations in the area that we could freely move around. That is to say, the area ranging between Vukovar and Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let me just return to the celebratory dinner after the fall of Vukovar. There have been various testimonies. What I'm interested in is whether this was, conditionally speaking, the only celebration, if I may call it so, or were there any others?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such festive dinners were organised on a number of occasions during this period. Several times they were held at Saponia, where I was quartered, but also in other places. A few humanitarian concerts were organised, in order to boost the people's morale and to provide some relaxation during the ravages of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, did you know who Franko Simatovic is, at that time; and did you know what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until then we had never met in person but I knew what he looked like from various meetings which both of us attended. And the same is true of Mr. Stanisic. I knew who they were and I knew what they looked like, but I never had a chance to be in any sort of direct communication with them, which means that they did not have a chance to know who I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say earlier meetings, what period do you have in mind? When were these meetings held?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean the period before 1991. I mean 1985 or 1986 or 1987. Because, as I said, I had completed the crime prevention school and many members of their service were the same generation as me during our education. So I had a chance to communicate with them, to socialise with them. During state celebrations or holidays, I had a chance to see them, and so on and so forth. Therefore, I knew them by sight, and I also knew them because of their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, you mentioned the dinners held after the fall of Vukovar and the awards that were distributed. Now let me ask you first about those which you attended. Did you ever see Franko Simatovic at any of these award ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of a dinner or celebration that you did not attend but which you heard Franko Simatovic did attend?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear that on any occasion Franko Simatovic was present at any of those dinners, or in the territory of Slavonia at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gagic. Can you please tell me the following. You have told us that you provided assistance in addition to deploying units in positions at the Bogojevo bridge. You said that, on the basis of your experience, you helped to establish police stations. Did you do any other sort of work? Did you go out into the field, and so on?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- in terms of organisation and operation, the police units had not been fully established but just a little bit in terms of regular policemen who were maintaining public law and order. And as the crime prevention police had not been established, traffic police only to a certain extent in the sector where I was, I, in fact, was involved in organising all of that. And at the orders of the TO Staff, through the commander of my unit, I occasionally visited places where some incidents of security interest took place, including the sites of some crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, before we have a look at the next document, please tell us about Saponia, where you were accommodated. Was the TO command also seated there? And who was staying there?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Saponia, the unit that I was a member of, with the belonging staff and leadership, was accommodated there. The commander of the TO Staff with his deputy and assistant and members of the special anti-terrorist unit, who were securing the commander and his deputy and also performed other tasks, were all accommodated there. There were several rooms in which occasionally people who had something to do with the TO staff stayed. There was a man who was a retired army colonel and who was in charge of de-mining, so he occasionally came and helped us with de-mining certain areas that we suspected included some mines and explosives. So mainly it was the unit staff and occasionally people that we engaged to perform certain special activities because we didn't have people who were trained to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The individual who was charged with training people in mine clearance, would he also go to the training centre in Erdut to conduct that same sort of training?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a retired army officer who we hired so that we would not be placing additional burden on the military personnel who had too much work to do anyhow on the front line, and he was supposed to check the terrain around Bogojevski bridge for any possible mines, because we didn't rule out that possibility that there were mines. He also had to do the same checks for mines of our billeting quarters and the facilities where Arkan's unit and the 101st Centre were housed. You see, around the area of the winery where these various units were housed, there were other facilities that were not directly connected to the work of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, let us look at Exhibit P1059. And while we're waiting for it to appear, Mr. Gagic, apparently the exhibit is a report of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence of the security department of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is under seal, Your Honours. Can we move into private session before it appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, I just want to check the transcript. You said Radovan Stojicic - this is line 23 on page 53 - he was the commander of the TO staff until the end of 2001. And then you said -- in what year was he no longer the commander?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think perhaps the error was mine. Actually, it was until 1991. Not 2001. So he was the commander until 1991. Not 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, become after that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, after that, became the chief of the State Security Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And did he come to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem after being appointed the chief of the service and the deputy minister in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Radovan Stojicic continued to visit the Eastern Slavonia area. I saw him there personally on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know why he went to that area in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to effect the takeover of duty with the newly appointed commander of the TO staff, Zivko Trajkovic, and this process of hand-over of duty lasted for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In 1992, in that area, were there any events of interest from the security point of view?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that area, there are always events that were of security interest, so perhaps you could be a little bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware whether, in 1992, the territory of the Republic of Serbia was threatened; and, if so, what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that central Serbia, or, actually, the territory of the Republic of Serbia, was under threat because of the incursion of a terrorist group from the area of the Republic of Croatia. The name of the action was Amfibija, and the territory where they came was in the area of Sombor and Apatin in a vehicle that was able to cross water and move on land, and the purpose was to commit a terrorist act, to blow up the -- the Erdut bridge close to which my unit was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know who led this action; and, if you do know, who was in that group of people who participated in that action?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The action was personally led by Radovan Stojicic, Badza, although he was already the chief of the department and deputy minister. The action was carried out by members of the special anti-terrorist unit, the SAJ, by members of the local police, and a certain number of police members and volunteers from the Krajina were also engaged in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to note for the record that there is nothing in the witness's summary that would suggest that he would provide this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you would permit me to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, it's -- it's on the record. Ms. Friedman noted it. I also noted that the last portion of the evidence that what's the basis of the knowledge of the witness is totally unclear. I'm not soliciting you to -- I'm not soliciting to or inviting you to clarify that. But I just put that on the record as well. That's -- Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the summary, it states that he was going to talk about Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and perhaps it's my mistake that I did not inform the other side in more detail. But if you permit me, I'm going to ask the witness about what he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you should have started with that. But, of course, to say, to testify about Badza, of course, that would be good for anything between one and 50 hours of testimony, without further precision. Well, if you consider it is of such importance that we should know it -- you've asked for three and a half hours. That's what is granted. Make your own priorities, I would say. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about this Amfibija action and the incursion. Where do have you this information from?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incursion is something that is well known. It was covered in the media. And we also had official information about the incursion of the group. We were informed as a unit who was securing the bridge, that such a group had made the incursion, and we offered our co-operation that we should engage members of our units in further proceedings so as to neutralise the activities of that terrorist group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And did you have any direct information from Radovan Stojicic, Badza?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At the time, we did have that from Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and it was then that we offered to engage our units on those tasks, but he refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, did you hear from Radovan Stojicic, Badza, about any additional police engagement of police from the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard when we offered to participate in the action, and in view of the fact that our area was a high risk one and still a problematic one, there was a problem from Badza -- there was a comment from Badza that he didn't want to weaken the set-up in Slavonia and that he would engage volunteer policemen from the Krajina, if necessary, and I think that he actually did engage a group. Actually, I did know that he did engage a group of policemen, policemen and volunteers from other areas of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, quite apart from this Amfibija operation, were you aware of any other alleged events in 1992 which would have required Badza to engage police -- police forces?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, in fact. A large protest rally was scheduled for the 9th of March of citizens in Belgrade. On the 9th of March, a large rally of the opposition forces gathered in Belgrade. There were great many victims. This happened in 1991. So a year later, they wanted to mark the anniversary of this event, and they wanted to gather many tens of thousands of citizens. This protest rally, in fact, was announced as an attempt to topple the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were certain outside forces engaged at the time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, around a thousand policemen were engaged outside of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. They were members of the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The security situation was very precarious because of this particular rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know if these policemen hired from the outside were given any sort of documents by Serbian authorities; and, if so, what sort of documents?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were given official identification papers because, without them, they would not have been able to work in the Republic of Serbia. They received the same ID cards as had been given to all members of public security at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like us to have a look at D456 now. It was MFI'd because we were waiting for a translation. We have now -- the translation is 2D882. And can we have page 47 in B/C/S and 45 in English, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document was MFI'd provisionally, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that case, can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, what became of the -- of your unit when you returned on the 6th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back on my own. The entire unit stayed back and continued in their previous duties, i.e., providing security to the bridge and checking those passing through there. And it stayed in that area until October of 2002, by which time most of the old members of that unit had already returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I just have to check. You said October 2002 or was that an error?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. 1992 is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, you say that some remained. What do you mean by that? Did they ...

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of the unit remained there securing the bridge. A smaller part of the unit members was deployed in local police stations in the area of Slavonia. When, in October 1992, the unit was sent back, those policemen wishing to return in these police stations where they were deployed continued working there. I mean in Slavonia. After the withdrawal of all Serbian forces from Slavonia, some of these policemen remained working there under Croatian authorities in police stations that were situated in the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gagic. When you came here to The Hague, you brought us your military booklet to the proofing session; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could now have a look at Exhibit 2D1056. I apologise, Your Honours. We have sent this for translation. We will -- no. I'm sorry. I have been notified that we have managed to obtain the translation, so if we could please show the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is that your military booklet?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, is each of your military engagement from the date of issue -- or let me first ask you: When was this military booklet issued to you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This military booklet was issued to me at the moment when I was capable of serving the army. That is to say, 1971. My compulsory military service is recorded here, as well as my promotions during the regular service. Then my participation in manoeuvres after I had served compulsory military service. Then my deployment while I was a member of the reserve forces. And also my participation in the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now show the last page of this document. And can we please zoom in. Also the right half of the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, if I understand this properly, this period is recorded as participation in the war when you were attached to the TO Staff in Erdut. What does this document represent as a piece of evidence? I'm trying not to ask you any leading questions but can you tell us what is recorded in such booklets? It is participation in what sort of institutions?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This booklet contains a record of all military engagement of the holder of this ID, so all the activities that the holder was involved in are recorded here, if this had to do with military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would tender 2D1056 into evidence. And for the Prosecution, I can say that Mr. Gagic is in possession of the original. He showed us this once he arrived here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We have no objection. We will consider whether we would like to see the original and will communicate that, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
